name: Freshworks
summary: Candidates commonly report that Freshworks' engineering interviews include a coding test, problem-solving and design rounds, and a hiring manager conversation, with questions often grounded in building SaaS products such as Freshdesk and Freshservice for business customers. Freshworks publishes five values on its careers page, starting with 'We champion our customers', so for many roles the questions come back to the customer.
rounds: Online coding test or recruiter screen
Low-level or system design round (for experienced roles)
Hiring manager round on past work and customer focus
looks_for: We are empowered to make an impact
Understanding how businesses use SaaS products day to day
Clear communication with customers and teammates

questions.text: Tell me about a time you went out of your way to solve a problem for a customer.
covers: The customer and what they needed
What you did beyond your usual work, and why
The result for them, and anything you changed in the product or process

questions.text: Describe a time you held yourself or your team to a higher standard than anyone asked for.
covers: The standard and why it mattered
How you got there without slowing everyone down
What it prevented or improved

questions.text: Tell me about a time you put a team win ahead of getting credit yourself.
covers: The situation and your contribution
Why you chose to put the team first
What the team achieved

questions.text: Tell me about a bold change you proposed. How did you get people behind it?
covers: The change and the risk in it
How you built support: data, a small trial, allies
What happened, and what you'd do differently

questions.text: How would you design a help desk system that routes each support ticket to the right agent?
covers: Tickets arriving from email, chat and web, stored in one model
Routing by skill, language, current workload and priority
Escalation when a ticket waits too long, and reports for managers

questions.text: What does multi-tenancy mean in a SaaS product, and how would you keep one customer's data safe from another's?
covers: Shared database versus separate schemas or databases, with trade-offs
A tenant ID on every query, access checks and tests that prove isolation
Stopping one heavy customer from slowing the rest down

questions.text: How would you build service-level timers for support tickets that pause outside business hours and on holidays?
covers: Business calendars per customer, with time zones and holidays
Working out due times, and events that pause or restart the clock
Warnings before a breach, and edge cases such as a change in calendar

questions.text: A large customer says your product became slow after the last release. What would you do?
covers: Confirming it with metrics for that customer's account
Checking what changed in the release, and turning it off or rolling back if needed
Keeping the customer and their account team updated, then adding a performance test

questions.text: How would you design public APIs and webhooks so customers can connect your product to their other tools?
covers: Versioning, authentication and rate limits
Webhooks with retries and signatures
Clear documentation and not breaking existing integrations

questions.text: A customer on a yearly plan uses only a small part of the product, and renewal is three months away. What would you do?
covers: Understanding their goals and looking at usage data
An adoption plan: training, a champion inside their team, quick wins
Signs you'd watch to know whether renewal is at risk

questions.text: How would you decide what to build next for small-business customers compared with large enterprises?
covers: How their needs differ: simplicity and price versus control, security and compliance
Evidence: feature requests, reasons customers leave, revenue at stake
How you'd explain the trade-off on the roadmap

questions.text: Why Freshworks? Which of its products would you most like to work on, and why?
covers: A specific product and who uses it
What interests you about building software for businesses
How your experience fits

questions.text: Which Freshworks value do you relate to most, and when have you lived it?
covers: One value, named once
A short, specific example
Why that way of working matters to you

tips: Freshworks' first value is 'We champion our customers'; bring stories where you listened to a customer and changed something because of it.
Explore Freshdesk or Freshservice before the interview so you can talk about real screens and flows.
In design rounds, think in tenants: which data belongs to which customer, and how one heavy customer can't slow down the rest.
For sales and customer success roles, practise explaining a product's value in the customer's words, not as a list of features.
